capitals.note: History of Bhutan: 'The seat of government was at Thimphu' and 'The winter capital was at Punakha Dzong' (Punakha 89.864 E 27.584 N); Thimphu became the year-round capital in 1966. Ngawang Namgyal page (paraphrase): the Zhabdrung's base was western Bhutan around Thimphu (Cheri, Simtokha built 1629) and the Paro valley. The pages give no year for when either city became the seat, so one entry is kept from the 1616 base; Punakha is the winter seat until 1966.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's first Bhutan shape begins in 1636 but the Zhabdrung arrived in 1616. History of Bhutan: he 'arrived in Bhutan in 1616 seeking freedom from the domination of the Gelugpa subsect'; the Ngawang Namgyal page puts his base in 'western Bhutan' (as I read it, around Thimphu with the Paro valley to the west). The core is my reading of those valleys; the pages give no boundary. Ledger 1634 carries the growth to the whole country.

region.text: western Bhutan: the Thimphu valley (Cheri, Simtokha) and the Paro valley to the west

ledger.note: 1616: the Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal arrives from Tibet and founds the Drukpa state in western Bhutan. History of Bhutan: he 'arrived in Bhutan in 1616 seeking freedom from the domination of the Gelugpa subsect'; infobox 'Unification: 1616-1634'; the Ngawang Namgyal page has him 'left Tibet to establish a new base in western Bhutan' and Simtokha Dzong (1629) controlling the road between the Paro and Trongsa valleys. The pages name the valleys, not a boundary; the Paro and Thimphu core is my reading. Cliopatria starts the state only in 1636.

region.text: the rest of Bhutan beyond the western valleys (Punakha, Wangdue Phodrang, Trongsa and the east), unified by 1634

ledger.note: 1634: the unification of Bhutan is complete. Infobox 'Unification: 1616-1634'; the Ngawang Namgyal page says he first unified the warring fiefdoms 'in the 1630s' and 'would conquer and unify all of Bhutan'; History of Bhutan has 'In 1634 Ngawang Namgyal defeated' (the extract I read breaks off there). The end of the infobox range is the year, the land is the modern country minus the western valleys already held (my reading); the fiefdoms were not states.

1650: the Druk Desi period begins: after the Zhabdrung's death (1651, kept secret for 54 years) secular rule passes to the Druk Desi under the dual system with the Je Khenpo. Infobox 'Druk Desi period: 1650-1905'; the Ngawang Namgyal page: 'died in 1651, and power effectively passed to the penlops'. History of Bhutan says 'in 1907, the fifty-fourth and last Druk Desi was forced to retire', so the infobox's 1905 end disagrees with that page by two years. The state, its colour and its dossier continue.

ledger.note: 1700: Bhutan invades Sikkim again. History of Bhutan: 'In the 1680s, Bhutan invaded Sikkim in pursuit of a rebellious local lord' and 'In 1700, Bhutan again invaded Sikkim'; the Kalimpong page says the 'Bhutanese encroachments had been in effect for about two decades' by 1706. The page names no battle; the Kalimpong hill tract is my reading of the ground fought over.

Held until the Treaty of Sinchula in 1865.

region.text: Cooch Behar (Koch Bihar), the plains state south of Bhutan

ledger.note: 1765: Bhutan treats Cooch Behar as its dependency. History of Bhutan: 'By the mid-1760s, Thimphu considered Cooch Behar its dependency'; the year is my reading of 'mid-1760s' and is tied to the Cooch Behar page's 1765 seizure. The Mughal-era background (Cooch Behar a Mughal vassal from 1609; its raja sought Bhutan's help against the Mughals in 1730) is not a Bhutan territorial event.

1765: Bhutan seizes direct control of Cooch Behar's Jalpeswar, Mandas and Jalash. The Cooch Behar page: Bhutan took direct control of Behar territories, 'including Jalpeswar, Mandas, Jalash', in the reign of Dhairjendra Narayan (1765-1770); the Debraj of Bhutan arrested Dhairjendra Narayan and took him to Punakha. The page gives no month, and the region is the Cooch Behar state as the nearest named region. Reviewer sa-05-c: confidence 2, as the page dates the seizure only to the reign 1765-1770 and names three territories, not the whole state.

ledger.note: 1772: the East India Company comes to Cooch Behar's aid against Bhutan. History of Bhutan: the British 'invaded Bhutan in 1772-73' and drove the Bhutanese garrison out of Cooch Behar after the succession dispute; the Bhutan page dates the Company's attack on Bhutan to 1774 instead. The year is the History page's; the land is Cooch Behar.

ledger.note: 1784: the British hand the Bengal Duars back to Bhutan. History of Bhutan: 'In 1784, the British turned over to Bhutanese control Bengal Duars territory'. Bhutan held them to 1865 (the Dooars page: 'This region was controlled by the kingdom of Bhutan when British India annexed it in 1865'). The counterpart is the East India Company, carried as the British Empire.

region.text: the Assam Duars (the Kamrup, Darrang and Eastern Dooars)

ledger.note: About 1790: the Druk Desi takes the Assam (Darrang) Duars from the declining Ahom kingdom. The Dooars page says only 'the Druk Desi of Bhutan took possession of them in last phase of 18th century' while the Ahoms faced rebellions; the year 1790 is my bridge across that span (page silent on the year). Earlier the Darrang Duars were held by Bhutan for annual tribute to the Ahoms, who reclaimed them four months a year (Jayadhwaj Singha's reign).

notes: Written by sa-05-c on 2026-10-19 from nine opened Wikipedia pages (the page budget for 18 shapes is 9). (1) START YEAR. Cliopatria starts the state in 1636; the Bhutan infobox gives 'Unification: 1616-1634' and History of Bhutan has the Zhabdrung arriving in 1616, so identity.start is 1616 with a western-Bhutan core (two new keyframes, 1616-1633 and 1634-1635). If the colour/compile agents prefer Cliopatria's 1636, the 1616 found event and the two new keyframes are the only things to drop. (2) DUARS AND KALIMPONG. Every Cliopatria shape of 1636-1938 is the modern outline (about 40 k km2), but Bhutan lost 'almost one-fifth' of its area in 1865 (Dooars page; Duar War page 'a fifth'). Corrections for 1788-1864 therefore add the Kalimpong hill tract (1706), the Bengal Duars (1784) and the Assam Duars (about 1790, confidence 1) to the Cliopatria shape (1683-1787 stays 'ok' with the ledger adding Kalimpong and the Bengal Duars); the convention used is that a correction describes the shape at the span's first year and the ledger's dated events carry the changes inside the span (Kalimpong 1706, Cooch Behar 1765-1774, Bengal Duars 1784, Assam Duars 1790, 1841, 1865). Pre-1784 Duar holdings (Cooch Behar page: 'From the early 17th century the Kingdom of Bhutan came to control the fertile plains'; the same page and the Dooars page give the Western Dooars to Cooch Behar State 1586-1949) are not settled and are left out. (3) 1939-1952 SHAPES. These add about 30,500 km2 of Arunachal Pradesh (106 of 114 added cells by gazetteer.py). The NEFA page shows British Assam / Indian administration and does not mention Bhutan, so the shapes are cut back to modern Bhutan. Why Cliopatria drew them is unexplained; the Tibet dossier's ledger note books the Tawang tract (Monyul) as Tibetan and quotes the Tawang district page as saying Monyul was 'absorbed into the control of neighbouring Bhutan and Tibet'; a gap-filler could open Tawang district for Bhutan's role there. (4) PROTECTORATE. Bhutan was a British protectorate by the Treaty of Punakha, 1910 (Bhutan page; Bhutan-India relations page: 'became a protectorate of the British Raj'), and under Indian guidance by the Treaty of Friendship of 8 August 1949 (Bhutan page; the relations page also gives 9 August) until the revised treaty took effect on 1 January 2011 (2007 treaty).
